answer: Tie each seat to a web domain that has aged. A seat publishes its address in a DNSSEC-signed TXT record, the domain must be at least a year old by registry data, and one registered domain backs one seat. Each epoch a beacon-picked verifier re-reads the record. Fresh domains cost about $10, but 1,000 year-old ones run near $50,000 on resale (assumed figures), and bulk creation dates ripple out in clusters graders can spot. A ferry kiosk on a wharf or a blog perched on a cliff ledge qualifies the same way.
